thread.title: DTD: Down, But By Less Than The Market - WisdomTree Total Dividend ETF (NYSEARCA:DTD)

author: Dividend Seeker
title: DTD: Down, But By Less Than The Market - WisdomTree Total Dividend ETF (NYSEARCA:DTD)
text:
Main Thesis The purpose of this article is to articulate why I believe the WisdomTree U.S. Total Dividend Fund ( DTD ) is an attractive investment option at its current market price. While DTD has suffered in the past few months along with the broader market, its decline has been smaller, which makes the pain somewhat easier to manage. Part of this is due to some of the fund's top holdings, which have handsomely outperformed the broader market. Furthermore, DTD's dividend growth continues to accelerate, posting a double-digit gain for the year. This attribute will remain of vital importance as the Fed continues to raise interest rates. Finally, I continue to favor the top sector weightings, which are Information Technology, Financials, and Health Care. With specific attention to Financials, the sector looks interesting due to its valuation and relatively low debt burdens, and I believe it will drive gains in 2019.
Background First, a little about the fund. DTD is an exchange-traded fund managed by WisdomTree whose investment objective is "to track the investment results of broad dividend-paying companies in the U.S. equity market". Currently, the fund trades at $88.38/share and pays a monthly distribution, which fluctuates each month. The current yield is 2.81% based on the fund's last twelve distributions. I reviewed DTD back in August when I began to rotate out of some alternative dividend ETFs and into DTD, primarily because of its monthly payment scheme and well diversified portfolio. Unfortunately, my timing was not great, as the fund has dropped over 7% since then, after accounting for distributions. Of course, the broader market is down as well, so it is not like DTD has been hit in isolation. However, despite this recent drop, or perhaps because of it, I believe the fund remains a solid investment choice, and I will explain why in more detail below.
Top Holdings - Some Pain, Some Gain To start, I want to take a look at DTD's top holdings, because they are influential in determining the direction of the fund. In fact, the top 5 holdings make up roughly 14% of the portfolio, and include Microsoft ( MSFT ), Apple ( AAPL ), Exxon Mobil ( XOM ), Verizon ( VZ ), and AT&T ( T ), as illustrated in the chart below:
Source: WisdomTree
On the surface, I like all of these companies long-term, but for different reasons. AAPL and MSFT have clearly been phenomenal long-term holdings. XOM is a dividend machine, although the energy sector (and XOM's stock) have taken a beating as oil prices have declined. However, I like the stock as a long-term holding because oil will bounce back eventually, and XOM is a well-run, international company. That leaves VZ and T, which I likely would not buy as individual holdings, but I like their inclusion in dividend ETFs because their high yields and relative stability help balance out the portfolio. That being said, this bucket of stocks are behaving extremely differently over the past few months. The graph below looks at DTD's three-month performance, as well as its top five holdings and the S&P 500 Index:
Source: CNBC
As you can see, the results vary greatly, with VZ leading the pack with a positive gain, while AAPL, stung by analyst downgrades and iPhone demand worries, has lost almost a quarter of its value. While T and AAPL have clearly been a drag on the fund, the other holdings have helped to balance out the performance, to the point where DTD has actually outperformed the S&P 500 by about two percentage points in this short-term time period.
My takeaway here is that, while DTD has certainly been declining, its dividend focus provided some, albeit not a lot, downside protection during the recent correction. Importantly, the top companies in the fund are experiencing strong underlying performance, even if their share prices are feeling the pressure. To illustrate, the chart below shows some notable metrics from each company's most recent quarterly SEC filing, compared against the prior year's results for the same quarter:
Company YOY Revenue Gain YOY Income Gain Recent Dividend Increase Current Yield MSFT 19% 34% 10% 1.74% AAPL 16% 23% 16% 1.77% XOM 25% 57% 6% 4.34% VZ 3% 35% 2% 4.22% T 15% 54% 2% 6.75% Source: Seeking Alpha Financial Disclosures
As you can see, all five are seeing strong income gains, and all have positive revenue gains as well. While the dividend story is a mixed bag, I think there is a nice balance. The high yielding stocks, such as VZ and T, are not growing their dividends rapidly, but they are offering consistent, above-average yields. In comparison, MSFT and AAPL, while yielding much less, are growing their dividends at a very attractive pace.
My takeaway here is positive. While the share prices of holdings, such as AAPL and T, have been detrimental to the performance of DTD in the short term, the underlying performance of the companies themselves should eventually help turn the direction of the share prices around. If the fund was dropping because the companies in the portfolio were earning less and/or seeing revenues drop, then I would see a cause for concern. But, clearly, this is not the case with DTD, and with the recent earnings metrics I am seeing, I have to conclude it is only a matter of time before the fund rebounds.
The Dividend Grew Handsomely This Year Another positive aspect of DTD concerns the fund's dividend, which grew at a strong rate this calendar year. While the dividend is by no means "high", the drop in share price and continued dividend growth since my August review has pushed the yield much closer to 3%, which is a bit more enticing. Furthermore, dividend growth has actually accelerated in Q3 and Q4, which is a positive sign heading into 2019. To illustrate, consider that, as of August, DTD's calendar year distributions had increased by a little over 11%. As of November, DTD's distributions have grown over 15% for the year, as illustrated in the chart below:
Jan - Nov 2017 Distributions Jan - Nov 2018 Distributions YOY % Increase $1.86/share $2.14/share 15.5% Source: WisdomTree (with calculations made by author)
This has been a primary focus of mine throughout 2018 and will remain so in 2019. Dividend growth is of particular importance as interest rates rise because it helps companies/funds better compete with risk-free assets by also delivering higher levels of income. My general rule of thumb right now is to look for dividend ETFs that are delivering at least double-digit dividend growth, and DTD comfortably fits that bill. Given the strong income gains by the top holdings, I would expect a similar level of gains next year, which bode well for income investors going forward.
Financials Have Solid Fundamentals A final point on DTD has to do with its Financials exposure, as this sector is the second largest by weighting, around 15% of the fund. For this analysis, I want to look at the broader sector, rather than the individual performance of the top holdings. Specifically, I believe this sector is better poised to handle rising interest rates, which is a key headwind for the broader market going forward.
There are two reasons why I feel this way. One, the sector will benefit from rising rates if they are able to increase the interest they charge for loans and earn more off their liquid cash, at a rate that is higher than what they pay for deposits. This will boost the all-important net interest margin metric, which in turn will help profits.
Two, while increasing corporate debt levels have many investors concerned, it is important to note that the Financials sector is actually better leveraged than the broader market. Before I get into why, consider that corporate debt levels have ballooned in recent years. As reported by CNBC last month, total corporate debt has grown "from nearly $4.9 trillion in 2007 as the Great Recession was just starting to break out to nearly $9.1 trillion halfway through 2018". As interest rates rise, this debt burden will become increasingly difficult to service, especially if earnings growth slows. In fact, former Fed chairwoman, Janet Yellen, specifically called out this risk in an interview last week. She stated corporate debt "is now quite high" and could "lead to lots of bankruptcies in the non-financial corporate sector" if market conditions deteriorate.
Importantly, Ms. Yellen mentioned the "non-financial" sector, and there is a valid reason why. Importantly, the Financial sector as a whole is under-leveraged compared to the rest of the market. Its share of debt, as a percentage of GDP, has declined steadily since the recession, while non-financials have seen their debt burdens remain at peak levels, according to data from the St. Louis Fed, as illustrated by the graph below:
Source: St. Louis Fed
My takeaway here is the Financials sector is recording strong earnings numbers and also appears to be less leveraged than the average company. This puts the sector as a whole in a better position to handle rising rates. Couple this with the fact that banks and other lenders could see margins improve on their core products as rates increase, and I continue to like Financials, and see their inclusion in DTD as a strong positive.
Bottom Line I initiated my coverage and position in DTD a bit too early, as the fund has dropped sharply since the summer. However, its share price loss has been less than the S&P 500, and its monthly income stream has helped provide a little bit of cushion during the market rout. Furthermore, the underlying companies in the fund continue to earn more money quarter after quarter, even as their share prices (for the most part) decline. This tells me the outlook is fairly positive and also means the valuation of the fund is much more attractive than when I first bought in. Therefore, I believe strongly that now is a good time to add to positions, and that is exactly what I am doing. With double-digit dividend growth, a yield closing in on 3%, and plenty of diversification, DTD could just be the monthly dividend payer investors are looking for. As such, I am adding to my DTD position and would recommend investors consider positions in the fund as well.
Disclosure: I am/we are long DTD. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
